summary.headline: A bot-management wall (DataDome) returns HTTP 401 with an unrenderable JavaScript-only shell for every plain HTTP fetch to every page tested -- homepage and article pages alike -- for every agent identity tried, including the three OpenAI agents robots.txt explicitly names and allows — critical severity, Reconcile the bot-management layer with the site's own stated crawling policy: either configure DataDome to pass through the specific agents robots.txt already declares allowed, or update robots.txt to stop declaring agents allowed that infrastructure blocks unconditionally.

findings.title: A bot-management wall (DataDome) returns HTTP 401 with an unrenderable JavaScript-only shell for every plain HTTP fetch to every page tested -- homepage and article pages alike -- for every agent identity tried, including the three OpenAI agents robots.txt explicitly names and allows
findings.evidence:
A plain-HTTP fetch (no JavaScript execution) to https://www.wsj.com/ and to a live article (https://www.wsj.com/world/russia/putin-to-meet-trump-envoys-as-u-s-pushes-to-revive-ukraine-peace-talks-564945af) returns HTTP 401 with a 770-byte body containing only '

Please enable JS and disable any ad blocker

' and a script tag loading https://ct.captcha-delivery.com/c.js -- DataDome's challenge shell. No article text, headline, byline or markup of any kind is present; a non-executing fetcher receives nothing to parse. This is identical, byte-for-byte in structure, across seven agent identities tested directly against the article URL: Googlebot, GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, ClaudeBot, Claude-SearchBot, PerplexityBot and Bingbot all receive the same 401 DataDome challenge. Critically, robots.txt (see companion finding) explicitly names GPTBot, ChatGPT-User and OAI-SearchBot in its permissive 'Allow: /' group alongside Googlebot and Bingbot -- yet the delivery layer blocks these explicitly-permitted agents exactly as it blocks everyone else. The site's stated crawling policy and its actual infrastructure behavior are completely disconnected: robots.txt says yes, DataDome says no, unconditionally, to all of them. No headless-browser check was available in this audit environment to determine whether a JavaScript-executing agent (which DataDome is designed to filter for) would pass the challenge; what is confirmed is that no plain-HTTP retrieval path -- which is how the overwhelming majority of AI agents actually fetch content, including OpenAI's own named, robots.txt-permitted agents -- can reach a single page of this site.

reproduction.observed: 401, body is a 767-770 byte DataDome challenge shell, identical for Googlebot/GPTBot/OAI-SearchBot/ClaudeBot/Claude-SearchBot/PerplexityBot/Bingbot user agents
reproduction.expected: 200 with real article markup, at least for the agents robots.txt itself names as allowed

suggested_action.summary: Reconcile the bot-management layer with the site's own stated crawling policy: either configure DataDome to pass through the specific agents robots.txt already declares allowed, or update robots.txt to stop declaring agents allowed that infrastructure blocks unconditionally.
suggested_action.mechanism: A retrieval agent that respects robots.txt (as GPTBot, ChatGPT-User and OAI-SearchBot are documented to) will see 'Allow: /', attempt the fetch in good faith, and receive a 401 challenge shell every time -- the worst possible outcome for a would-be-compliant agent, and functionally indistinguishable from the site having disallowed it in the first place, except that the disallow was never actually stated.
steps: Confirm with the DataDome configuration whether verified, declared crawler IPs/user-agents (Googlebot, Bingbot, and the named AI agents) are meant to bypass the challenge, as is standard practice for major bot-management vendors.
If a bypass rule exists but is not firing, debug why (IP verification failure, UA string mismatch, etc.).
If no bypass is configured, decide deliberately whether these agents should be reachable at all, and make robots.txt match that decision.
suggested_action.verification: A plain HTTP fetch using GPTBot's or Googlebot's declared user agent, from a range DataDome can verify as genuine, returns real page content instead of a 401 challenge.

findings.title: robots.txt names all three OpenAI agents (GPTBot, ChatGPT-User, OAI-SearchBot) in the permissive Allow group, but Anthropic's and Perplexity's equivalent agents are named nowhere in the file and fall to the blanket 'User-agent: * / Disallow: /' group
findings.evidence: robots.txt opens with 'User-agent: * / Disallow: /' -- a blanket disallow for any agent not named elsewhere in the file -- then lists dozens of named exceptions grouped under a single 'Allow: /' block: all major search engines (Googlebot, bingbot, duckduckbot, baiduspider, etc.), ad/marketing crawlers, SEO tools, social-preview bots (facebookexternalhit, twitterbot, linkedinbot, Citoid, ZoteroTranslationServer), and -- in their own three-line block -- 'ChatGPT-User', 'GPTBot', 'OAI-SearchBot'. No equivalent lines exist anywhere in the file for ClaudeBot, Claude-User, Claude-SearchBot, PerplexityBot or Perplexity-User; none of the wildcard-catching group's exceptions match those names, so all five fall through to the opening 'Disallow: /'. The file states no rationale for naming one AI lab's three agents and omitting two others' five agents, and the omitted agents are the same class of retrieval/training agent as the ones explicitly allowed, not a different kind of traffic.

reproduction.observed: GPTBot, ChatGPT-User and OAI-SearchBot each appear on their own User-agent line inside the permissive Allow group; none of ClaudeBot, Claude-User, Claude-SearchBot, PerplexityBot or Perplexity-User appear anywhere in the file
reproduction.expected: Either all major AI labs' equivalent agent classes treated consistently, or a stated rationale for treating them differently

suggested_action.summary: Decide deliberately whether Anthropic's and Perplexity's retrieval agents should be allowed the same as OpenAI's, and update robots.txt to reflect that decision explicitly rather than by omission.
suggested_action.mechanism: As written, the file's policy toward AI agents cannot be read as a considered stance on 'AI crawling' in general -- it names one company's agents and is silent on two others', which is difficult to distinguish from an incomplete or outdated list rather than an intentional single-vendor allowance. This finding is independent of, and upstream of, the companion delivery-layer finding: even if DataDome is reconfigured to honor robots.txt, ClaudeBot and PerplexityBot would still be disallowed by this file as written.
steps: Confirm whether excluding Anthropic and Perplexity specifically, while allowing OpenAI, reflects a deliberate current commercial or policy decision.
If not, add ClaudeBot, Claude-User, Claude-SearchBot, PerplexityBot and Perplexity-User to the same Allow group as GPTBot/ChatGPT-User/OAI-SearchBot.
If so, consider stating the rationale in a comment, as the file already does for its overall automated-collection notice at the top.
suggested_action.verification: Every major AI lab's retrieval and training agent names are either all present in the Allow group or all absent, with a stated reason for any deliberate exception.

opportunities.title: The declared XML news sitemap already exposes headline, publication date and canonical URL for every recent article, independent of the HTML delivery block -- this is a real, reachable surface worth building on rather than a coincidence to ignore
opportunities.rationale: https://www.wsj.com/wsjsitemaps/wsj_google_news.xml returned a clean 200 with real content to the same plain-HTTP fetch that gets a 401 DataDome challenge on every actual article URL. Each <url> entry carries <news:title>, <news:publication_date>, <lastmod> and a canonical <loc>. This means an agent that cannot read a single WSJ article can still correctly learn that a specific headline exists, when it was published, and its canonical URL -- a meaningfully better outcome than the total blackout the HTML layer presents, and evidence that WSJ has not blocked machine-readability everywhere, just at the content layer.
opportunities.mechanism: Extending what the sitemap already exposes (e.g. a one-paragraph dek/summary field, already common in news sitemap extensions) would let a citing assistant correctly attribute and describe a WSJ story -- headline, date, and the fact that it exists behind a subscription -- even while respecting the paywall on the full text, closing part of the gap this audit's crawl-access findings describe without touching the subscription model at all.
steps: Confirm the news sitemap's summary/dek field is populated (this audit's sample did not show one) or add one if not present.
Consider whether this sitemap-level metadata should also appear as JSON-LD on the (currently unreachable) article pages themselves, for the case where the delivery-layer finding above is resolved.

not_assessed.check: Rendering fidelity, JS-dependency ratio, viewport occlusion and Core Web Vitals (render-extractability-audit)
not_assessed.reason: Requires fetching real page HTML/DOM to compare against, and no page -- homepage or article -- returned anything but the DataDome challenge shell to this audit's plain-HTTP fetches. No headless-browser engine (Playwright/Puppeteer) was available in this run's environment to test whether a JavaScript-executing client passes the challenge; without one, this audit cannot determine whether these checks would even apply differently than the plain-fetch case.
not_assessed.impact: Cannot say whether WSJ's actual article rendering (for a session that clears the DataDome challenge) is JS-dependent, fast, or free of layout-shift and occlusion problems -- only that no non-JS-executing fetch gets far enough to find out.

not_assessed.check: Structured data completeness -- JSON-LD (NewsArticle, Organization), Open Graph, Twitter Card, phone/address extraction (structured-data-audit)
not_assessed.reason: No page markup was reachable to parse.
not_assessed.impact: Cannot verify whether WSJ marks up its articles with NewsArticle/Article schema, byline, publish date, or social-preview meta tags -- markup that, if present, would matter more than usual here since it is likely the only machine-readable surface of an article that survives the bot wall (see the sitemap-derived opportunity below, which is a distinct, and reachable, XML surface, not HTML markup).

not_assessed.check: Answerability -- question-coverage, definitional clarity, quotable-fact density, question-shaped structure, claim attribution (answerability-audit)
not_assessed.reason: Requires readable prose from actual pages; none was reachable.
not_assessed.impact: Cannot assess whether WSJ's journalism is quotable/extractable prose (it almost certainly is, by any human editorial standard) -- only that no automated, non-authenticated agent can read it to find out.

not_assessed.check: Freshness and corroboration signals -- dateline markup, self-description, identity anchors (freshness-corroboration-audit)
not_assessed.reason: Requires page HTML; none was reachable via plain fetch. Note: the sitemap-derived opportunity below does supply a lastmod/publication_date per article at the XML level, independent of this check, which looks at in-page signals specifically.
not_assessed.impact: Cannot verify in-page date/byline markup quality on articles.

not_assessed.check: On-site engagement -- LCP/CLS/TBT, above-the-fold content, interaction affordances (engagement-audit)
not_assessed.reason: Requires either a real page load or a headless-browser render; the plain fetch used elsewhere in this audit cannot measure rendering performance, and no headless-browser engine was available in this run's environment.
not_assessed.impact: Cannot assess the on-site experience for a session that does pass the challenge (a real subscriber, or Google's own JS-executing indexing pipeline, which is why WSJ still ranks in Google search despite this audit's plain-fetch findings).

not_assessed.check: Whether WSJ's actual subscription/login paywall is itself well-behaved for AI discoverability (e.g. whether it exposes a teaser, structured summary, or licensing signal the way some paywalled news sites do)
not_assessed.reason: This was the specific mechanism this audit run set out to test (a genuinely auth-gated site, as distinct from a pure bot-wall). It could not be reached: the DataDome bot-management layer blocks every plain-HTTP request before any content-level paywall logic is ever reached, for every agent identity tried. This audit cannot see past DataDome to observe whether a real subscription paywall exists behind it, or what it does.
not_assessed.impact: This is the honest, and itself informative, outcome: for this site, the practical distinction between 'hard paywall' and 'bot wall' that this audit set out to compare against nytimes.com collapses, because the bot-management layer is the first and only thing any automated, non-JS-executing agent ever encounters, regardless of what content-access policy sits behind it.
